name: The Four Color Theorem
statement: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so no two neighbours match.
meaning: Any map drawn in the plane, or equivalently on a sphere, can be coloured with at most four colours so that no two regions sharing a border segment receive the same colour. Four colours always suffice, no matter how the map is carved up, and some maps genuinely require all four.
mechanism: Adjacency means sharing a boundary of non-zero length, not merely touching at a single corner where several regions meet — a distinction that is essential, since otherwise many regions could meet at a point and no bound would exist. Turn each region into a vertex and join two vertices whose regions share a border; the result is always a planar graph, so colouring the map becomes colouring a planar graph with four colours. The proof reduces the infinitude of maps to a finite set of configurations that every map must contain, then shows none can appear in a minimal counterexample.

examples.text: Whenever four regions each share a border with the other three, they need four distinct colours — the reason three colours cannot suffice in general and the bound is four.
A pie of many wedges meeting only at the centre can be coloured with two alternating colours, illustrating why adjacency requires a shared border of real length, not a single shared point.
The bound of four is special to the plane and sphere; on a torus, up to seven colours can be required, so the theorem is a statement about flat maps specifically.

variants.name: The five color theorem
variants.text: The weaker statement that any planar map can be coloured with five colours, which has a short proof checkable by hand, unlike the four-colour result.

variants.name: The formal Coq proof
variants.text: Gonthier and Werner's 2005 formalisation of the entire proof in the Coq proof assistant, which reduced the trust required to the correctness of the proof-checker's kernel.

whyItMatters: It is a landmark of graph theory and, more famously, the first major theorem proved with substantial computer assistance, which forced mathematicians to debate whether a proof no human can fully survey still counts as a proof. That methodological question, not any doubt about its truth, is its lasting significance.

working.text: for any planar map, take four colours as sufficient to separate all neighbours, and never reach for a fifth.
turn a colouring problem into planar graph colouring by making regions vertices and shared borders edges.
apply the four-colour bound only to the plane or sphere, since other surfaces like the torus need more.

limits: Its scope is the plane and sphere; other surfaces require different numbers of colours, a torus needing up to seven. The controversy it sparked was methodological, not mathematical: because the 1976 proof reduced the problem to a large set of configurations checked by computer, it could not be verified by hand, raising the question of whether an un-surveyable proof is a genuine proof. That concern about method has been largely settled on the correctness side by the 2005 machine-verified formalisation; no serious doubt remains that the statement is true.
misreadings: It applies only to flat maps — on curved surfaces the number of colours needed changes. And the debate it caused was about what counts as a proof, not about whether the theorem is correct; its truth is not in doubt, especially after the formal machine-checked proof.
origin: Conjectured by Francis Guthrie in 1852; Alfred Kempe's 1879 proof was accepted for over a decade until Percy Heawood found its flaw in 1890; finally proved by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken at the University of Illinois in 1976, with computer assistance.
